memories.content: Use the same term throughout the proposal for the same interaction concept or interface element.
Use abbreviations only for recurring terms of three or more words.
Present the full name and abbreviation together when using an abbreviation for the first time.
Prioritize the research role over diagnostic labels or deficits when referring to participants.
Reviewers from different subfields struggle to infer undefined abbreviations from context alone.
Use the term formative evaluation for studies seeking design modification evidence, and distinguish it from final efficacy judgments.
The user can have contribution labels such as principles, models, or guidelines approved only if they align with the abstraction level of the actual deliverables.
Design principles describe the relationship between conditions and outcomes rather than serving as instructions that merely replicate a single screen layout.
Use an em dash only for a deliberate interruption or sharp contrast; otherwise split the sentence or choose ordinary punctuation.
In procedural passages, begin each sentence with the action, condition, or output instead of repeating “we” so the steps remain easy to follow and reuse.
Write system behaviors confirmed in the actual usage environment as observed states.
Write system behaviors not yet confirmed in the field as conditional plans.
Readers can reconstruct a sequence more accurately when each sentence begins with the action or condition rather than the author.
Do not mechanically split connected thoughts into separate short sentences when doing so destroys the intended reading rhythm.
Preserve a longer sentence when its clauses form one continuous movement that is easier to follow together than apart.
The user understands that short sentences are easier to scan but feels that uniformly segmented prose loses its reading rhythm.
Write procedural sentences so their opening phrase can be reused as a checklist item without changing the step's meaning.
The user should choose “I” as an individual author or “we” for a named team and should not mix them when describing the same responsible party.
Action-first procedural sentences can be reordered or copied into a checklist more easily because their subject is the step rather than the proposal author.
The user can explain whether an em dash marks an intentional interruption or contrast rather than using it decoratively.
An em dash creates a stronger interruption than a comma and can make a deliberate contrast easier to hear in the sentence.

analysis.overview: The frames cover separate, complementary areas of proposal writing without making scope-aligned claims about the same operational decisions. The reference focuses on terminology, participant descriptions, study framing, and contribution labels; the compared frame focuses on punctuation, procedural structure, evidential phrasing, sentence rhythm, and authorial voice.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful reference-only naming rule with no compared-side claim addressing terminology for concepts or interface elements.
relations.summary: Use one consistent term for each interaction concept or interface element throughout a proposal.

relations.reason: This reference-only rule governs when abbreviation is warranted, a decision not addressed by the compared frame.
relations.summary: Reserve abbreviations for recurring terms containing at least three words.

relations.reason: The reference memories state the first-use rule and its reader-centered rationale; the compared frame contains no corresponding abbreviation-introduction policy.
relations.summary: Introduce an abbreviation alongside its full name because cross-subfield readers may not infer an undefined abbreviation reliably.

relations.reason: This is a standalone reference-only policy for participant descriptions, absent from the compared frame.
relations.summary: Refer to participants by their research role before diagnostic labels or deficits.

relations.reason: This reference-only terminology rule governs study purpose and evaluation framing, which the compared frame does not address.
relations.summary: Call studies formative evaluations when they seek evidence for design modification, distinguishing them from final efficacy judgments.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful reference-only criterion for selecting contribution labels, with no compared-side counterpart.
relations.summary: Approve contribution labels only when their abstraction level matches the actual deliverables.

relations.reason: This reference-only claim defines the proper abstraction of design principles and is not restated in the compared frame.
relations.summary: Treat design principles as relationships between conditions and outcomes, not instructions reproducing one screen layout.

relations.reason: The compared memories jointly supply the usage rule, its audible effect, and the test of deliberate intent; the reference frame has no em-dash policy.
relations.summary: Use an em dash only for an intentional interruption or sharp contrast whose stronger break can be explained, choosing ordinary punctuation otherwise.

relations.reason: The compared memories split one procedural-writing policy across its form, readability rationale, and reuse benefits; the reference frame does not address procedural sentence openings.
relations.summary: Begin procedural sentences with the action, condition, or output so sequences remain clear and steps can be reordered or reused as checklist items.

relations.reason: The compared memories provide the two complementary evidence conditions of one behavior-reporting policy, which has no reference-side counterpart.
relations.summary: Express system behavior as an observed state when confirmed in actual use and as a conditional plan when field confirmation is absent.

relations.reason: The compared memories state the rule, its continuity criterion, and the user preference motivating it; the reference frame contains no sentence-segmentation policy.
relations.summary: Preserve connected clauses in a longer sentence when splitting them would damage a continuous, easier-to-follow reading rhythm.

relations.reason: This is a standalone compared-only policy for consistent authorial voice, not addressed by the reference frame.
relations.summary: Use “I” for an individual author or “we” for a named team, without mixing them for the same responsible party.

reports.compared_only: Compared-only guidance covers purposeful em dashes, action-first reusable procedures, evidence-sensitive behavior claims, preservation of sentence rhythm, and consistent authorial pronouns.
reports.reference_only: Reference-only guidance covers consistent terminology, controlled abbreviation use, participant-centered descriptions, formative evaluation, and contribution labels matched to deliverable abstraction.
